q: Banyan adds a second firewall model and points it at the syslog input already used by the first firewall. Its events are stored, but a rule that searches the firewall index for blocked connections never returns them. What is the most likely cause?
options: The new device inherited the shared input's default source type and index
The new device's events were dropped by an ingest-time filter on the input
The new device sends over UDP, so its events were lost before they arrived
The new device's events are still waiting in the indexing refresh interval
explanation: An input applies its default source type and index to everything that arrives on it, so a new device on a shared port is labelled and routed as the old one, with the wrong time rules and container. A drop filter would mean the events were never stored, but here they are present.

q: An analyst knows a server sent authentication events at about 09:30 today, but a search of 09:00-10:00 returns none. Searching all time finds them, with ingest time 09:30 today and event time in 2019. What does this pattern indicate?
options: The events were routed to an index the analyst has no permission to read
The indexing layer delayed the events beyond the search window and applied a default event time when the new index was made available
The events were filed by a wrong or misread timestamp from the source side
The events were duplicated upstream and the copies replaced the originals
explanation: The events arrived on time (ingest time 09:30) but were filed under a wrong event time, from a bad source clock or a timestamp the SIEM misread, so a search of the right window cannot find them. An access problem would hide them from the all-time search as well.

q: Events from twenty branch routers are relayed through one central syslog server to the SIEM. Every event shows the same value in the host field. What explains this?
options: The routers share one source type, which overwrites the host label
The SIEM recorded the relay as host instead of reading it from the message
The relay merges events from all routers into a single multi-line record
The routers are synchronised to the same clock, and SIEM host attribution treats matching clock sources as a shared device identity
explanation: For relayed data the sender the SIEM sees is the relay, so unless the ingestion layer takes the host name from inside each message, every event is labelled with the relay's name. A shared source type sets parsing rules, not the host label.

q: A source averages 1,000 events per second with an average event size of 800 bytes. Approximately how much raw data per day will it add before indexing overhead or replication?
options: About 0.8 GB per day
About 6.9 GB per day
About 86.4 GB per day
About 69.1 GB per day
explanation: 1,000 x 800 bytes = 800,000 bytes per second; multiplied by 86,400 seconds this is about 69.1 x 10^9 bytes, or 69.1 GB per day. 86.4 GB/day is the figure for 2,000 EPS at 500 bytes, not this source.

q: An application's audit records are written as several records per block. A threshold rule counting failed logons from it fires far less often than the application's own report suggests it should. Which ingestion fault best explains the under-count?
options: The breaking rule splits each record into several one-line events
The breaking rule merges several real records into one stored event
The input truncates each record at the platform's maximum event size
The routing rule sends the records to a cheaper, slower storage tier
explanation: If the breaking rule merges several records into one stored event, a count-based rule sees one event where several logons failed, so it under-counts. Splitting records would produce more events, not fewer, and tiering affects search speed, not counts.

q: In Splunk, events from a newly onboarded source land in the correct index but are cut in the middle of records and carry wrong _time values. Which single setting most likely explains both symptoms?
options: The sourcetype assigned to the data, which selects breaking and time rules
The index assigned to the data, which selects its retention and access
The host value assigned to the data, which selects the relay to trust
The _indextime recorded for the data, which selects the search window
explanation: In Splunk the source type selects the line-breaking and timestamp rules, so a wrong source type corrupts both at once. The index is correct here and governs retention and access, not how events are broken or timed.

q: Proxy logs make up most of Banyan's ingest volume and the finance team wants costs cut, but beaconing detection relies on every proxy record. Which option reduces cost while keeping every record available to an investigator?
options: Aggregate the proxy logs into hourly request counts per host
Drop proxy requests to well-known content delivery networks
Trim the URL and user-agent fields from every proxy record
Route the proxy logs to a cheaper storage tier with slower search
explanation: Moving data to a cheaper tier keeps every record and only slows searching, the lowest-risk option. Aggregation destroys the per-request timing that beaconing detection needs, and dropping or trimming permanently removes evidence.

q: Rendered Windows events include a long block of descriptive text that is identical in every event of the same ID. Which volume-reduction step targets this with the least loss of evidence?
options: Aggregating the events into counts per event ID per host per hour
Drop the event IDs that take the most space and keep full descriptions for every other event type in the channel
Trimming the repeated description while keeping the structured fields
Routing all rendered Windows events to an archive-only storage tier
explanation: Removing repeated boilerplate while keeping structured fields cuts size without removing what detections use. Aggregation and dropping lose individual events, and an archive-only tier keeps everything but makes it hard to use for detection.

q: During a cost review an engineer proposes an ingest-time rule that drops all PowerShell Operational events because they are 'noisy'. What is the most defensible way to handle the proposal?
options: Treat it as a detection change: list dependent rules, assign an owner and review date
Approve the drop if a temporary recovery buffer keeps rejected events for seven days, without checking the rules that consume them
Approve it if the endpoint agent still keeps the events in its local event log
Treat it as housekeeping and record it in the SIEM platform's change log only
explanation: A drop rule removes evidence for every future detection and investigation; this one would also remove script-block events recording an intruder's commands. It must be decided per event type with dependent detections, an owner and a review date. Local logs on endpoints roll over and are not centrally searchable.

q: After reloading the Banyan dataset, a health query returns total 341 and distinct_raw 340 from SELECT COUNT(*) total, COUNT(DISTINCT raw) distinct_raw FROM events. What does this show?
options: One event failed to parse and was stored twice, once raw and once parsed
One event was stored twice because the ingestion layer does not de-duplicate
One event was dropped and replaced with a placeholder row by the loader
One event's raw text was truncated at the maximum event size and split
explanation: Two rows share identical raw text, so one event was stored twice. load() has no de-duplication, so a duplicate line, as at-least-once delivery can produce, is stored and counted. A truncated and split event would give two different raw values, not identical ones.

q: In a scratch copy of the kit, one truncated JSON line is inserted into banyan_events.jsonl. After load raises a JSONDecodeError, a count of the events table returns 0, although the file has 340 valid lines. Why is the table empty?
options: SQLite rolls back the whole transaction when any inserted row is invalid
The idx_ts index cannot be built when one row has no timestamp value
The table is dropped first and all lines are parsed before any insert
The search command refuses to read a table left by an incomplete load
explanation: load() runs DROP TABLE IF EXISTS first, then parses every line into a list in memory before inserting, so an exception on one line aborts the load after the old data is already gone. No row was ever inserted, so there was nothing for SQLite to roll back.

q: A threat model notes that anyone able to write to an upstream log file can insert one malformed record into a feed. Which ingestion property most directly prevents this from blinding the SOC to the whole feed?
options: Recording ingest time beside event time on every stored event
De-duplicating events on a stable identifier before they are written
Routing the feed to a container with restricted search access
Quarantining and counting bad records while ingesting the rest
explanation: Isolation contains a fault to the one bad record: it is quarantined, tagged and counted while the rest of the feed keeps flowing. Without it, all-or-nothing ingestion is a denial-of-service condition. De-duplication improves count accuracy but does nothing for malformed input.

q: In minisiem, logon_type and the VPN country are present in the dataset but are not among the twelve stored columns. What is the practical consequence for a detection rule that needs them?
options: The rule must extract them from raw at search time, which is slower and fragile
The rule cannot use either field because a value without a dedicated column is discarded before the original event can be searched
The rule can use them directly, because SQLite creates columns on first use
The rule must wait for a reload, because raw is only populated on request
explanation: The fields survive only inside the raw column, so a rule must pull them out with json_extract at search time, which is slower and easier to get wrong. They are not discarded, precisely because the original line was kept.

q: The minisiem volume query shows the proxy producing about 83 per cent of stored bytes while Sysmon events are the largest on average. Before trimming proxy data, what should the SOC establish first?
options: Whether Sysmon events could be trimmed instead because they are larger
Which detections, such as beaconing or large uploads, depend on proxy fields
Whether the proxy can send its events in a more compact binary format
Which proxy users generate the most requests so they can be excluded
explanation: High-volume network data often feeds important detections, so any reduction must start by asking which rules and investigations use it. Trimming the largest events per record ignores that proxy data dominates total volume, and excluding heavy users removes the very activity beaconing produces.

q: A covered entity in India routes its VPN logs into a container with a 30-day retention because the container is cheap. Why is this routing decision a compliance problem and not just a storage choice?
options: The DPDP Act 2023 forbids storing VPN logs outside a restricted container
MITRE ATT&CK T1562 requires authentication logs to be kept for one year
CERT-In's 2022 directions require ICT logs to be kept for a rolling 180 days
ISO 27001 requires every security log to be kept in a hot searchable tier
explanation: The container carries the retention period, and CERT-In's April 2022 directions require covered entities to keep ICT system logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, so routing a regulated source to 30-day storage breaks that duty. T1562 is an adversary technique, not a retention rule.

q: A platform team moves Windows Security events from index wineventlog to a new index win_security to separate retention. Nothing errors, but several rules stop producing alerts. What most likely happened?
options: The new index has a shorter refresh interval, so events arrive too quickly
The new index inherited a different source type, breaking timestamp rules
The rules still name the old index, so they now search an empty container
The new index restricts access, so rules run as the analyst cannot read it
explanation: Detection rules usually name the container they search, so when routing changes and the rules do not, they search where the data no longer is and fall silent without any error. Changing the index does not by itself change the source type or its time rules.

q: A VPN appliance buffers events during an outage and delivers a two-hour batch late. The SIEM stores only event time. What can the SOC not determine as a result?
options: Whether the batch's events occurred during the outage window
Whether a correlation rule ran before the batch's events had arrived
Whether the batch's events can be searched by their original time
Whether the late records were assigned to the expected source type when the collector sent the queued batch to the SIEM
explanation: Without ingest time a late batch looks identical to a timely one, so the SOC cannot measure lag or tell whether a rule evaluated its window before all events arrived. Event time still places the events correctly in time and still allows searches by when they happened.

q: A SIEM's syslog input accepts UDP from any address on the internal network. A red-team report shows forged events planted in it from a test workstation. Which control best addresses the weakness?
options: Authenticate the input with TLS client certificates and restrict which networks reach it
Raise the input's maximum event size so forged records are split and easier to spot
Route the input's events to a restricted container that only the SOC can search
Record ingest time on the input so that forged events show an unusual lag value
explanation: Forged events succeed because the input accepts anyone who can reach it; authenticating senders and restricting the network, plus alerting on unexpected senders, closes that gap. Restricting who can search the data does nothing to stop forged data being written.

q: Source-health monitoring alerts when any source's event count drops sharply, and nothing else. Which ingestion attack does this configuration fail to detect?
options: An intruder stopping the endpoint agent on a compromised server
An administrator deleting the input that receives firewall events
A flood of junk events that exhausts licence and delays real events
A routing change that makes one event type disappear from its index
explanation: Flooding raises volume, so monitoring that only watches for falls misses it while the backlog delays the events that matter and the licence quota drains. A stopped agent, a deleted input or a routing change that removes an event type all reduce volume and would be caught.

q: A health check compares event time with ingest time. Several events from one host carry event times three days after their ingest times. How should the SOC treat this?
options: As normal lag, since buffered events always arrive with later timestamps
As expected, because ingest time is assigned before the event is created
As harmless, because the events are still searchable within all-time scope
As a red flag for a wrong clock or deliberate time manipulation to investigate
explanation: An event cannot be ingested before it happened, so a negative gap means either a faulty clock or timestamps set to file events where nobody looks; both deserve investigation. Normal lag produces event times earlier than ingest times, not later.

q: During onboarding of a new EDR feed, the engineer wants to prove that no events are being silently lost between source and SIEM. Which check gives that assurance most directly?
options: For a fixed window, compare the source's sent count with the SIEM's stored count
For a fixed window, compare the stored count from the new endpoint feed with the same window on the preceding business day
For a sample of events, compare the host field with the source's own host name
For a sample of events, compare event time with the source's own system clock
explanation: Reconciling what the source says it sent against what the SIEM holds for the same window directly measures loss. Comparing with yesterday only shows a change in volume, and host and time checks test labelling, not completeness.

q: During a large incident the SIEM is under heavy load. A forwarder confirms delivery of a critical event, but an analyst's search run seconds later does not return it. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The event was delivered but routed to a container the analyst cannot read
The event is stored but not yet searchable because indexing has lagged
The event was rejected by the input because it exceeded the size limit
The event was de-duplicated against an earlier copy and discarded
explanation: Indexing is not instantaneous: new data becomes searchable after a refresh interval, and that delay grows under heavy load, so a delivered event can be briefly unsearchable. A rejected or discarded event would not resolve itself, while this one appears once indexing catches up.

q: minisiem's load() creates only one index, idx_ts on the ts column. Why is a time index the first choice for almost every SIEM store?
options: Because event time is the only field present in every source type
Because SQLite requires an index on a time column before inserts
Because almost every search is bounded by a time range
Because indexing by time makes duplicate events easy to remove
explanation: SIEM searches are almost always limited to a time window, so organising and indexing by time lets the engine skip everything outside it. SQLite requires no index at all, and a time index does nothing to identify duplicates.

q: An analyst used to Splunk's _indextime is investigating ingestion lag in Elastic data that follows the Elastic Common Schema. Which field holds the comparable value?
options: @timestamp
@timestamp, the mapped occurrence time
event.dataset
event.ingested
explanation: The Elastic Common Schema defines event.ingested for the time the event reached the pipeline, the counterpart of Splunk's _indextime. @timestamp is the event time, and TimeGenerated is Microsoft Sentinel's event-time column.

q: Banyan's proxy logs reveal which websites individual staff visit. The SOC needs them for detection, and the privacy officer cites the DPDP Act 2023. Which ingestion design best serves both needs?
options: Drop the URL field at ingest time so no browsing history is ever stored
Route proxy logs to a container whose search access is limited to the SOC
Route the proxy logs to a shared default index and rely on each analyst to limit searches to records relevant to their own team
Aggregate proxy logs into daily totals so individual visits are not kept
explanation: Separate containers allow access to sensitive data to be limited to those who need it, which supports DPDP safeguard duties while keeping the evidence. Dropping URLs or aggregating would protect privacy but destroy the detail that detections such as beaconing need.
